vignette: Three years ago, a sudden arrhythmia sends Arthur, now seventy-eight, to his kitchen floor. He watches the ceiling tiles spin as his vision grays, feels the violent compression of his chest, and hears the absolute silence that follows when the cardiac monitor flatlines. He wakes in the ICU to tubes, alarms, and a cardiologist speaking in slow, deliberate syllables. The physical recovery takes months, but his internal architecture never reboots. Now, his days are governed by invisible checklists. He wakes at 4:15 a.m., pulled from sleep by a heart stutter. He checks the door locks twice, then three times. He measures his pulse with a medical watch, logs the numbers in a leather-bound notebook, and circles any reading that deviates by more than five beats. When the numbers spike, his chest tightens, and he is instantly back on that kitchen floor, certain the flatline is returning. He stops watching the news. He stops reading fiction. He tells me stories demand hope, and hope is a variable he can no longer control. His work as a database administrator, once a source of quiet satisfaction, has become a fortress. He configures redundant server backups with obsessive precision. If a single node lags, he reroutes traffic, resets connections, and stares at the progress bars until they hit one hundred percent. He tells me he does it to "ensure data integrity," but I notice how his breathing deepens only when the system confirms success. The work is structured, predictable, and forgiving-unlike his own body. He begins to speak of his heart in technical terms: latency, bandwidth, firewall breaches. He tracks the ping times of distant servers like a man tracking his own breath, searching for the exact millisecond something might falter. He treats his physiology like legacy code that refuses to compile. He lives alone in a house his ex-wife packed up two years ago, long before the arrest, though he frames the move as a necessary precaution. He purchases a second medical watch. He deletes his email notifications. He tells me that uncertainty is a vulnerability he patched out of his life years ago, but his body runs on unpatched code now. He no longer invites anyone over. Grocery trips happen on weekdays, timed to avoid crowds and long lines. When a cashier asks how he's doing, Arthur gives a clipped response and walks quickly to the exit. He stops calling his daughter. He tells me she asks too many questions, that she looks at him with worry, and worry, he says, is just anxiety wearing a different name. He doesn't say that he looks at his own reflection in the bathroom mirror and sees a machine that might break down without warning. In session, Arthur's fingers tap a steady rhythm against his thigh, mirroring the arrhythmia he fears. He describes a recent dinner where the host's kitchen timer sounded like a defibrillator. He leaves without finishing his meal, hands shaking, convinced he is losing control of a system he can no longer fully trust. He stops driving past the hospital. He sits in his armchair, watching the rain, waiting for a symptom that never quite arrives, but always might. The session clock ticks toward the end. Arthur stands, adjusts his sweater, and smooths the lapel of his jacket. He thanks me for the hour, his voice steady, his gaze fixed on the door. He will walk to his car, count his steps, and check his pulse at the red light. He has built a life around monitoring, predicting, and controlling what once surprised him. He leaves the room, closes the door behind him, and steps into the quiet.
